A Great AIrony

There is a great irony in what has become of the academic field of artificial intelligence. Many of us who have spent our lives studying artificial intelligence are driven to understand what a mind is, and how it works. Some of us came here by studying linguistics; some neuroscience; some the theory of computation; some philosophy of mind; some really like programming robots. We imagined that publishing our work would help other scientists and the public better understand what it is that a mind is, how it works, and in the process share our love for language, brains, and the fundamental truths of computation. We imagined AI tools that would free people from their responsibilities—freeing minds to learn and grow once we fully understood a task enough to automate it.

Yet it seems the primary effect of our work has been a hemorrhaging of human understanding and autonomy.

This is particularly salient in 2026, as we outsource increasingly important work once core to our identities (our work, interpersonal communication, logistical advice, emotional support, problem solving, critical thought) to frontier AI systems. This all feeds the significant AI backlash. But it has been going on a long time. Coding as a Way of Knowing

I love coding. Like many other programmers, including the coding agents, I was trained in an environment with satisfying coding challenges and and visual design. For much of my life, being able to turn concepts into software was the ultimate demonstration of mastery.

Writing code was the ultimate demonstration of mastery: being able to write software to do matrix algebra, was the ultimate demonstration that you knew what matrices are. Using your own software to make things work is not write a game engine was the ultimate demonstration of knowing what matrices mean in graphics.

You know how it is often said you don’t truly know something until you can teach something (to your grandmother)? Well, the ability to operationalize a task so precisely that even a computer, the densest possible student, could understand—that was the ultimate test of understanding.
